note: Examines the institutional machinery the Act creates, the AI Office, the Board, the scientific panel and national authorities, rather than the obligations themselves. Useful for anyone asking who actually enforces it.
title: The EU AI Act: A framework for collaborative governance
explain_beginner: The European Union passed a major law called the AI Act to regulate how artificial intelligence is built and used across its member countries. This paper looks past the headline rules and asks a more practical question: who actually makes sure the law works day to day, and how do all those different bodies coordinate with each other? The Act does not rely on just one regulator. Instead it sets up a whole system, including a new European AI Office, an advisory forum bringing in outside voices, a panel of independent scientific experts, and a separate national authority in each EU country. The paper studies how this network of bodies is meant to work together, arguing that a genuinely shared, collaborative style of governance is starting to take shape rather than one central authority simply issuing orders downward. It takes a balanced view, pointing out real strengths in this collaborative design as well as specific weaknesses and open questions about whether so many different bodies, at both the EU and national level, can stay consistent and effective in practice.
explain_business: For a company operating in or selling into the EU, this paper matters less for the AI Act's substantive rules, which it does not focus on, and more for understanding who a business will actually deal with when it comes to compliance and enforcement. Rather than one central AI regulator, the analysis shows the Act creates a layered system, an EU level Office and advisory and scientific bodies alongside a separate competent authority in each member state, meaning a company selling AI systems across multiple EU countries could face somewhat different practical enforcement experiences country to country under the same underlying law. The author's own critical view, that this collaborative structure has real strengths but also open questions about consistency, is a useful signal for compliance teams to expect some early inconsistency or friction as these bodies get up and running, rather than a single, uniformly applied rulebook from day one. Businesses should track guidance from both the EU level Office and their relevant national authorities separately, since the paper suggests these layers will not necessarily move in lockstep.
explain_practitioner: This paper is a legal and institutional analysis of the European Union's AI Act, examined using its April 2024 agreed text, rather than an empirical study. Instead of cataloging the Act's substantive obligations on AI developers and deployers, the author focuses on its governance architecture, the European Artificial Intelligence Office, an advisory forum, an independent scientific panel, and national competent authorities in each member state, and how these bodies are meant to coordinate risk based oversight across the EU's single market. The central argument is that this multi-body structure reflects an emerging model of collaborative governance, meaning shared enforcement rather than a single top down regulator, and the paper frames this both as a strength, since it draws on varied expertise and keeps authority closer to national contexts, and as a risk, since consistency across many bodies is harder to guarantee. A limitation evident in the paper's own framing is that it offers a critical perspective identifying potential weak points rather than empirical evidence on how the system performs, since the analysis predates full operation of the Act's institutions.
